headline: Bunker Blitz Turns Execution Rocks Into a Bluefish Highway
subhead: The stripers here are running small and scattered while blues crash bunker pods from the Neck to Matinecock — here's where to find both.
body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island had his coffee going cold Tuesday morning, asking me the same thing three other guys had asked before him: "Where'd all these blues come from all of a sudden?" I told him what I've been telling everybody this week — they didn't come from anywhere. They've been sitting on that bunker the whole time. You just had to be looking in the right spot at the right tide to see it.

And the right spot, this week, has been the stretch from Throgs Neck out through Execution Rocks. I ran out Thursday morning on the tail of the outgoing and found bunker balled up so tight off Matinecock Point they were pushing rings on the surface, gulls working them from above, and blues underneath cutting them to pieces. Nothing subtle about it — you could see the slicks of oil on the surface from two hundred yards. Threw a Hopkins No-Eql off the transom into the edge of the bait and had a hook-up before it hit bottom. Blues running 4 to 8 pounds, a few bigger, and they didn't care what you threw at them — diamond jigs, bunker spoons, topwater poppers if you wanted to make it interesting. The water temp at Kings Point is reading right around 71 degrees, a couple degrees warmer than what they're seeing out past New London, and that gradient matters. Warm water on this end is holding the bait tight to the western structure — Exy Rocks, the Stepping Stones rockpiles, the Throgs Neck rip — instead of letting it spread out and thin. Concentrated bait, concentrated blues. Simple as that.

Now here's the honest part, because I'm not going to sell you a bill of goods. The bigger bass just aren't here in the numbers you'd want this time of August. The real cow action has been trailing east all summer — anything approaching slot size is mostly staying out past New Haven where the water's a shade cooler. What we've got in the Western Sound right now is schoolie bass, 18 to 24 inches mostly, mixed right in with those bluefish on the same structure. Execution Rocks on the outgoing is still doing what it's always done — current pulls bait off that rockpile and the bass sit right on the downcurrent side waiting for it. White bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how hard that tide is ripping, tipped with a strip of bunker belly, has been the most consistent producer. Don't overthink it out there. Drift the edge, keep contact with bottom, and let the current do the work.

We called this one last week — said the building tidal flow running into the new moon on the 12th would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened at Exy Rocks and the Throgs Neck rip. That extra push on the moon tides has the bait moving with more purpose, and the fish that are around are using it.

Fluke fishing has been modest — I want to be straight about that. It's not a bad bite, it's just not a banner one. Best results have come drifting the channel edge off Hempstead Harbor and the mouth of Manhasset Bay in 20 to 30 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the incoming tide pushing you along. You'll pick through some shorts to get a keeper, but the ones coming over the rail have been decent, 18 to 22 inches, a few better. Incoming has outfished outgoing on the fluke pretty consistently this week — cleaner water, and the bait gets pushed up onto those flats instead of pulled off them.

Weakfish, I'll be honest with you, are a shadow of what this Sound used to produce. I remember when you could load a cooler with tide-runner weaks off Hart Island in August and not think twice about it. These days you're lucky to pick off two or three keeper-class fish at dusk working the edge of Little Neck Bay on a bucktail tipped with a piece of squid or Fishbites. It's not nothing — but don't plan your whole trip around it. Treat it as a bonus if you're already out there for bass or blues at last light.

Porgies remain the one bottom bite you can count on without a lot of head-scratching. Stepping Stones and the reef structure around Hart Island have been holding fish all week — sandworms or clam on a high-low rig, anchor up tight to the rocks, and you'll keep bent rods most of the tide. It's not glamorous fishing but it fills a cooler, and on a week when the bigger bass are playing hard to get, that counts for something.

Blackfish are still off the table for most of you right now with the summer closure in effect through this stretch of the Sound — worth noting for the guys already asking, because that bite will matter again once the fall season opens and water starts cooling into October.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for the bunker to leave Matinecock or Execution Rocks anytime soon — that thermal edge holding around Kings Point should keep bait stacked tight to structure through the week, and the blues will keep working it as long as it's there. If the nights start cooling off even a little heading into the back half of August, I'd expect some of those bigger bass currently staged east to start filtering back this direction on the tide changes — that's the pattern I've watched play out for thirty years on this water. Until then, fish the outgoing at Exy Rocks for schoolies and blues together, and don't be afraid to burn some gas checking Matinecock and the Neck rip on the way — that's where the bait is, and where the bait is, that's where you'll find fish worth bending a rod over.
